issues.legal_issue: Income from temporarily letting commercial assets remains business income when the letting is a temporary mode of exploiting those assets and the business is not abandoned.
material_facts: The company had operated a textile-manufacturing business and stopped manufacturing after incurring heavy losses and accumulating substantial liabilities.
Under a court-approved arrangement with creditors, the company let its business assets to a lessee to help meet its liabilities.
The lease was for a fixed term with an option of renewal, after which the assets would revert to the company.
The company maintained the assets and a skeleton staff, did not dispose of the assets, and was found to intend to resume business after the temporary suspension.

The Tribunal considered the relevant facts and found that the company intended to exploit its commercial assets temporarily rather than permanently part with them; the Supreme Court found that conclusion plausible and sustainable.
issues.conclusion: The lease income was assessable as profits and gains of business, not as income from other sources. The High Court was right, and the revenue's appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The character of income from letting assets depends on how the owner exploits them and, principally, on the intention inferred from all the circumstances. Under Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax v. Shri Lakshmi Silk Mills Ltd., a commercial asset does not cease to be such merely because it is temporarily let instead of used by its owner. Commissioner of Income Tax v. Calcutta National Bank Ltd. likewise treats the issue as dependent on the circumstances. Narain Swadeshi Weaving Mills v. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax and Commissioner of Income Tax v. Shaw Wallace & Co. explain that business involves a real and organised course of activity. Inland Revenue Commissioner v. Broadway Car Co. and New Savan Sugar and Gur Refining Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax illustrate that a letting that evidences a decision to part with the business or its assets may instead yield rental income. The Court applied sections 10 and 12 of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922, concerning the relevant heads of income, and discussed section 24 in explaining the significance of business-income classification for setting off losses.

rule.if: income_classification_proceeding and commercial_asset_used_in_business and temporary_letting and intent_to_resume_or_continue_business and tribunal_finding_plausible

predicates.income_classification_proceeding: The proceeding determines whether income received from letting assets is business income or income from another source.
predicates.commercial_asset_used_in_business: The owner acquired and used the let asset as a commercial asset in its business.
predicates.temporary_letting: The owner let the asset for a limited period rather than disposing of it permanently.
predicates.intent_to_resume_or_continue_business: The owner intended the letting to be a temporary suspension or mode of exploiting the asset, not an abandonment of its business.
predicates.tribunal_finding_plausible: The fact-finding tribunal considered the relevant circumstances and reached a plausible conclusion about the owner's intention.

issues.definition: When an income-classification proceeding concerns a commercial asset used in business, a temporary letting intended to preserve or continue the business, supported by a plausible factual finding, results in the lease income being classified as business income.
